A specially appointed judge sided with Apple in the company's lawsuit seeking documents from 14 federal agencies as part of its defense against the Department of Justice's antitrust lawsuit. Here are the details.

Some background

Last May, Apple asked the court hearing the DOJ's antitrust lawsuit against it, filed in 2024, to compel the following 14 federal agencies to turn over documents related to how they evaluate, purchase, and use smartphones and wearable devices:

  • The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • The Department of Commerce
  • The Department of Homeland Security
  • The Department of Defense
  • The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • The Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • The General Services Administration
  • The Department of Labor
  • The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • The National Security Agency (NSA)
  • The Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • The Office of Management and Budget
  • The Office of Personnel Management
  • The Department of State

Apple argued in its request that these records could help support its defense against allegations that iPhone policies are anticompetitive.

In short, Apple's argument is that if federal agencies choose its products based on their security, privacy, or other features, this supports the argument that the challenged practices are legitimate product advantages rather than anticompetitive restrictions.

The government, however, opposed Apple's request, arguing that the agencies are irrelevant to the case, neither regulate smartphones nor purchase or use them in the same way as ordinary consumers.

The government asked the court to seal the subpoenas, saying they were both irrelevant and overly burdensome, and noted that they could involve privileged, classified, or nationally sensitive information.

The court then referred the dispute to retired federal judge Jose Linares, who, serving as a special discovery master, was responsible for deciding whether Apple could compel the subpoenas.

In complex cases involving extensive discovery, courts sometimes appoint special masters to handle narrower disputes to reduce the workload of the presiding judge. Special masters can be retired judges, practicing attorneys, or other experts with relevant experience.

Apple granted permission to seek documents from federal agencies

Judge Linares has now ruled in Apple's favor, finding that all of its document requests are relevant to the core allegations in the case. Additionally, he noted that the government failed to provide substantive reasoning for its broad opposition.

Although the special discovery master sided with Apple, this does not mean the company will immediately receive all the documents it requested.

Instead, agencies can still refuse to disclose specific records they believe are privileged or otherwise protected, but must identify them on a privilege log. Any disputes arising from this could trigger a new round of discovery disputes, including possible ex parte review by Judge Linares.
